query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of W by V to form a single-phase BCC NbMoTaWV (with low-level V, e.g., 5–15 at.%) will improve room-temperature ductility by lowering lattice friction for 1/2<111> screw dislocations and increasing grain-boundary cohesion, while retaining high-temperature mechanical performance and irradiation resistance comparable to equiatomic NbMoTaW.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy; single-phase BCC; polycrystalline; excellent mechanical performance at 1600 °C; very poor room-temperature ductility; irradiation resistance primarily inferred from first-principles.
generation.intervention: Composition microalloying: replace a small fraction of W with V (targeted composition NbMoTaW(1−x)Vx, x ≈ 0.05–0.15), followed by homogenization (≥1200 °C) and recrystallization to retain single-phase BCC and equiaxed grains.
generation.conditions: Synthesis by vacuum arc melting or induction melting under high-purity Ar; total O, N, C impurities kept as low as practicable; homogenization at 1200–1400 °C for ≥12 h; recrystallization anneal to obtain equiaxed grains (10–50 µm); confirm single-phase BCC by XRD/EBSD; comparative testing at identical strain rates and specimen geometries.
generation.structural_mediator: A stable single-phase BCC solid solution with V uniformly distributed: (i) reduced average shear modulus and Peierls barrier for 1/2<111> screw dislocations; (ii) potential weak segregation of V to grain boundaries that increases cohesive energy; (iii) absence of embrittling intermetallics (σ, Laves) and maintenance of high chemical disorder.
generation.mechanism: At room temperature, BCC RHEAs often exhibit high lattice friction for screw dislocations leading to brittle fracture. Introducing V lowers the lattice friction stress and facilitates screw dislocation glide, enabling more homogeneous plasticity and suppressing cleavage initiation; modest improvement in grain-boundary cohesion further mitigates intergranular cracking. At 1600 °C, deformation is dominated by dislocation glide/climb and diffusion; the strong solid-solution strengthening from Nb/Mo/Ta/W is largely retained, and the small V fraction does not significantly reduce high-temperature strength. Under irradiation, the high chemical disorder and associated defect recombination pathways are preserved; V is not expected to introduce embrittling radiation-induced phases, so swelling and irradiation hardening remain comparable.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to equiatomic NbMoTaW: (RT) measurable increase in uniform and total tensile elongation and a shift in fracture mode from predominantly cleavage to more ductile or mixed fracture; yield strength may decrease slightly due to reduced lattice friction but with net gain in ductility. (1600 °C) compressive strength and creep resistance remain within a modest margin of the baseline (no substantial degradation), with similar strain-rate sensitivity. (Irradiation) comparable levels of irradiation-induced hardening, defect cluster density, and swelling; no new radiation-induced embrittling phases.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic NbMoTaW: single-phase BCC, excellent mechanical performance at 1600 °C, minimal ductility at room temperature, irradiation resistance primarily supported by first-principles predictions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis holds if: (i) the alloy remains single-phase BCC after V addition and heat treatments; (ii) V content stays low (≈5–15 at.%) to avoid σ/Laves formation; (iii) impurity levels (O, N, C) are minimized to prevent interstitial embrittlement; (iv) grain size and test strain rate are comparable to baseline. It may fail if phase separation occurs, if substantial interstitial contamination raises the DBTT, or if processing induces significant short-range ordering that reintroduces pinning.
generation.uncertainty: There is limited direct experimental evidence here; the exact magnitude of ductility improvement and the tolerance window for V content are uncertain. It is possible that V could slightly reduce high-temperature strength or alter irradiation response, and the degree of V grain-boundary segregation is composition- and processing-dependent.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two alloys: (A) equiatomic NbMoTaW (baseline) and (B) NbMoTaW(1−x)Vx with x ≈ 0.10. Melt under high-purity Ar, homogenize at 1300 °C for 24 h, recrystallize to equiaxed grains (~20 µm). Verify single-phase BCC by XRD and EBSD; assess microchemistry and GB segregation by EPMA/STEM-EDS. Conduct: (1) RT tensile tests (same geometry, strain rate); (2) compressive tests at 1600 °C; (3) heavy-ion irradiation (e.g., Fe or Kr) to a fixed dpa at an intermediate temperature (300–500 °C), then measure hardness changes and defect structures.
measurements: STEM-EDS/EPMA for composition uniformity and GB segregation
RT engineering stress–strain curves, yield strength, uniform and total elongation, fractography (SEM)
1600 °C compressive stress–strain and creep rate under constant stress
Nanoindentation or microhardness pre- and post-irradiation
TEM of irradiation-induced defect clusters/dislocation loops and swelling/voids
DSC/DTA to detect any ordering or phase transformations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if any of the following occur relative to the baseline: (i) no statistically significant increase in RT ductility (uniform or total elongation remains effectively negligible and fracture remains predominantly cleavage); (ii) a substantial degradation of 1600 °C mechanical performance (e.g., clear, large decrease in strength or increase in creep rate beyond modest experimental scatter); (iii) irradiation produces noticeably higher hardening, defect cluster density, or new radiation-induced phases in the V-added alloy.
